what_its_for: Romiplostim is used to raise your platelet count if you have a condition called immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Platelets are tiny blood cells that help your blood clot. When your platelet count is too low, you can bleed more easily. This medicine helps your body make more platelets to lower your risk of bleeding.
how_to_take: Romiplostim is given as a shot (injection) under your skin, usually in your belly, thigh, or upper arm. A doctor or nurse will give you this injection once a week in a clinic or doctor's office. Do not try to inject this medicine yourself unless your doctor has specifically trained you to do so. Each injection is given on the same day each week if possible.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose based on your weight and your platelet count. The usual starting dose is 1 microgram per kilogram of your body weight once a week. Your doctor will check your blood regularly and may increase or decrease your dose to keep your platelet count in a safe range. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss your weekly injection, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to double up on doses or give yourself an extra injection to make up for the missed one. Your doctor will advise you on when to get your next dose.
storage: Romiplostim should be stored in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it. If it has been accidentally frozen, do not use it. Once the medicine is mixed (reconstituted) and drawn into a syringe, it should be used within 24 hours if kept refrigerated or within 4 hours at room temperature. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Do not use it if the solution looks cloudy or has particles in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid activities that could cause injury or bleeding, such as contact sports or rough physical activity, especially when your platelet count is low. Avoid taking aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other blood-thinning medicines unless your doctor says it is okay, as these can increase your bleeding risk. Tell all your doctors and dentists that you are taking romiplostim before any procedure or surgery.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: unusual or heavy bleeding (such as bleeding gums, nosebleeds that won't stop, blood in your urine or stool, or coughing up blood), sudden severe headache or vision changes, weakness or numbness in your arms or legs, chest pain or shortness of breath, leg pain or swelling (which could be signs of a blood clot), or if you develop swelling or pain in your belly. Also call if you notice signs of infection such as fever, chills, or feeling very unwell. Report any new lumps, bone pain, or night sweats to your doctor.
when_it_works: Romiplostim usually starts working within 1 to 2 weeks of your first injection. Your platelet count should begin to rise during this time. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to monitor your progress. It may take a few weeks of dose adjustments before your platelet count reaches the right level. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor, even if you feel well, because your platelet count can drop quickly after stopping.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known if romiplostim is safe during pregnancy. A pregnancy registry exists for women who take this medicine while pregnant. Children: Romiplostim can be used in children aged 1 year and older with ITP. The dose is based on the child's weight. Older adults: Older adults can use this medicine, but should be monitored closely since they may have a higher risk of blood clots. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as close monitoring may be needed.
